item.title: The Gleaners
item.lesson: Gleaning — gathering the stalks left after harvest — was an ancient legal right of the rural poor, and the lowest work in the fields. Millet, a farmer's son, painted three women bent to it with the monumental dignity other painters gave to goddesses: massive silhouettes against a golden distance where the real harvest is stacked in plenty they will not share. When it appeared at the Salon of 1857, less than a decade after the upheavals of 1848, bourgeois critics recoiled — one sneered about 'the three Fates of pauperism' — because dignity granted to the poor read as politics, and it was. Millet's Realism insisted that modern art's proper subject was the actual life of actual people, a claim that runs straight through Courbet to van Gogh, who copied Millet obsessively and called him 'father Millet.' Note the composition's quiet cruelty: the women's bent backs never touch the horizon line of abundance behind them.
item.lookFor: Far right, in the background haze, a man on horseback watches the field — the steward, overseeing both the harvest and its leftovers. Power in this painting is small, distant, and mounted.
